Ubiquity of Christ’s Body
yoo-BIK-wi-tee uhv krysts BOD-ee
noun
From Latin ubique, everywhere; the Lutheran doctrine that Christ’s human body is omnipresent, framed to defend consubstantiation.

📖 Biblical Definition

The ubiquity of Christ’s body is the Lutheran doctrine that the human body of Christ, by virtue of its union with His divine nature, partakes of the divine attribute of omnipresence, and so is or may be present everywhere—a teaching framed chiefly to defend the bodily presence of Christ in, with, and under the bread of the Lord’s Supper (consubstantiation). The Reformed churches reject this doctrine as contrary to Scripture and to the Chalcedonian definition of Christ’s two natures. Scripture teaches that Christ has a true human body, like ours in all things save sin, and a true human body is by nature local, occupying one place; it was born, grew, was crucified, rose, and ascended bodily, and the angels declared, He is not here: for he is risen. He was received up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God, whom the heavens must receive until the times of restitution of all things—words that locate His body in heaven, not everywhere. The two natures are united in one Person without confusion: the divine remains divine, omnipresent; the human remains human, local; the properties of one nature are not transferred to the other. To make Christ’s body ubiquitous is to confound the natures, swallowing up His true humanity in His deity. The dictionary names the ubiquity of Christ’s body as a Lutheran error, framed to prop consubstantiation, which violates both the plain teaching of Scripture on Christ’s ascended body and the Chalcedonian confession of His two unconfused natures.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Lutheran doctrine that Christ’s human body is omnipresent, framed to defend consubstantiation; rejected as confounding His two natures and denying His ascended, local body.

📖 Key Scripture

Mat 28:6 — "He is not here: for he is risen, as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord lay."

Act 3:21 — "Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began."

Act 1:11 — "Which also said, Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The doctrine of ubiquity confounds Christ’s two natures to prop consubstantiation; Scripture confesses His true, local human body, ascended and seated in heaven.

expand to see more

The ubiquity of Christ’s body is itself the corruption this entry names: a Lutheran doctrine, devised to defend the bodily presence of Christ in the Supper, which teaches that His human body partakes of the divine omnipresence and so is everywhere. The error springs from a true premise wrongly applied—the union of the two natures in one Person—by transferring the property of the divine nature (omnipresence) to the human nature, which is precisely what the Chalcedonian definition forbids: the natures are united without confusion or change. To make the body ubiquitous is to swallow up Christ’s true humanity in His deity, leaving Him not truly man.

Scripture holds the line. Christ took a true human body, made like unto His brethren in all things, that He might be a merciful high priest (Heb 2:17); and a true human body is local, occupying one place. The angel said of that body, He is not here: for he is risen (Matt 28:6); He was taken up into heaven (Acts 1:11), whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things (Acts 3:21). His body is therefore in heaven, at the right hand of God, not everywhere. The Reformed confess His real spiritual presence in the Supper by the Holy Ghost to the believing soul, without dragging His body down from heaven or stretching it everywhere. The ubiquity doctrine, framed to prop consubstantiation, must be refused as contrary both to the Scriptures on His ascended body and to the confession of His two unconfounded natures.
